questions.explanation: #17 says adoption funding should prioritise grants, whether via development or individualized outreach, that put ZEC in the hands of users whose needs will grow its ongoing use, and #19 says ZECsy onboards people face to face. The first option is the airdrop picture that #19 calls a strawman. The last option runs against #18, which says the world will not adopt Zcash by convincing today's crypto users.
options: Mass distributions of ZEC to anyone who signs up, with success judged by the number of new wallets that are created.
Larger payments to existing holders and developers, on the theory that committed insiders are the most reliable route to adoption.
Grants for direct, individualized outreach that gets ZEC to people who really need it and will keep using it in their communities.
Marketing aimed at today's crypto users, who already understand wallets and exchanges and can be persuaded quickly.
questions.prompt: Supporters said the ZIP's adoption funding is not about airdrops. What kind of spending did they say they had in mind instead?

questions.explanation: #3 and #5 say holders' money should not fund things that do not benefit them, #15 says examples the ZIP calls intentionally provocative put the fund's support at risk, and #51 adds that Zcash is a currency, not a charity. #42 says the objection is to the purposes, not any recipient, which is why the third option misreads it. The ZIP itself says the stream continues at its existing value and all examples can be funded legally (#1, #14).
options: The examples describe activity that is unlawful in most jurisdictions, so funding them would expose coinholders and the fund to legal risk.
Money taken from coinholders should go to what benefits them, and deliberately provocative examples risk alienating the holders the fund depends on.
The named groups are undeserving of help, whatever a grant to them would achieve for Zcash adoption or for the people involved.
The ZIP enlarges the funding stream and extends its duration beyond what ZIP 214 currently provides, taking more from holders than before.
questions.prompt: Critics objected to the list of example recipients in the ZIP. Which description fits the objection as the critics themselves stated it?

questions.explanation: #17 and #19 say the proposal is individual outreach, not airdrops, and #16 says the study polled crypto people who do not have these use cases. The third option is tempting but is the reply in #26 to a different challenge, the demand for a guarantee that recipients keep using ZEC. The pilot idea comes from #46, and no supporter agreed to hold payments until it ran.
options: They disputed the figures, saying that far more than a quarter of the airdrop recipients in that analysis had become lifetime active wallets.
They accepted the figures and agreed that no payments should be made until a pilot programme under ZCG had produced data of its own.
They said retention is irrelevant because recipients may freely sell ZEC for fiat, so no guarantee of continued use should ever be required.
They said the ZIP does not propose airdrops, that ZECsy-style outreach differs, and that the study polled crypto users who lack these use cases.
questions.prompt: An analysis of over 2 million airdrop wallets was cited as evidence that giving away ZEC rarely creates lasting users (#15). How did supporters of the ZIP answer it?

questions.explanation: #51 raises the administrators' competence and no later post replies to it. The guarantee point was repeated in #7, #13 and #37 and accepted in #9. The money point was disputed in #6, and the conflict-of-interest point was answered in #30 and #32, so both remain contested rather than unanswered.
options: That the people administering a grant programme are not necessarily equipped to evaluate humanitarian need or to administer financial assistance.
That the ZIP guarantees funding to no one, leaving every applicant to be accepted or rejected through the committee's normal grant process.
That money from the Dev Fund is taken out of users' pockets, so those who spend it owe holders and users a fiduciary duty.
That a contributor's existing grant creates a conflict of interest around the ZIP, which coinholders should weigh when they decide.
questions.prompt: Which of these points was raised in the thread and then went without a response from any participant?

questions.explanation: #47 links the ZECsy grant thread to show professional, transparent milestone reporting, while #42 and #44 ask what success metrics justified the original approval and ask ZCG to weigh in; no ZCG reply appears. No audited figures or pilot results were posted, and the only study cited (#15) was used against the approach, which #16 rebuts as polling crypto people. #48 answers a related point by saying ZIP 1015 already requires target metrics.
options: Audited retention figures from ZECsy participants were posted; the unanswered request was why developers are excluded from the fund.
Results of an earlier ZCG pilot programme were cited in support; the unanswered request was which groups should count as debanked individuals.
A link to the grant's milestone-reporting thread was offered; the concrete metrics behind the original approval, asked of ZCG, were not given.
A study of existing crypto users was cited in its favour; the unanswered request was what renaming the fund would cost.
questions.prompt: What support was offered in the thread for ZECsy's track record, and what evidence did a critic ask for that never appeared?

questions.explanation: #26 grants that selling for fiat is possible, rejects a guarantee as inappropriate and impossible, and rests the case on exposure making future use more likely. The first option borrows the developer point #20 made against the ZIP, which no supporter used as a defence. The third misreads #6, which only denies that the money is taken from users' pockets.
options: Fiat conversion is harmless because ZCG-funded developers already convert nearly all the ZEC they receive, so recipients should be treated no differently from them.
Exposure to ZEC as a useful part of someone's life makes future use more likely; no onboarding can guarantee it, and demanding a guarantee would mean never onboarding anyone.
Because the funds already exist in the protocol, how recipients spend them is nobody's concern, and the outcomes of the grants need not be examined at all.
Conversion proves the recipients are real users, since selling for fiat shows they are finding a way to spend the money in their daily lives.
questions.prompt: Critics asked whether recipients might simply swap ZEC for fiat (#20). Which is the strongest argument actually made in reply?

questions.explanation: #36 accepts the point in #34 and argues that its protection depends on the ZEC being held or spent as ZEC, which a publicly recorded grant converted to fiat does not provide, so the fund should pay for payment tooling and off-ramps instead. The first option contradicts #36, which agrees debanking risk is real. The third overstates the airdrop data in #15 and #46, which concern incentive programs rather than every payment.
options: Debanking risk is overstated because exchanges rarely freeze ordinary accounts, so the extra friction of using ZEC outweighs any protection it offers to recipients.
Sex workers rarely need privacy tools in practice, so the money would be better spent paying wallet developers than paying recipients, whatever their circumstances.
Airdrop statistics show that any distribution of ZEC to individuals fails, so no payment of any kind to anyone can drive adoption of the currency.
The privacy benefit holds only while ZEC stays ZEC; a public grant cashed out to fiat is back in the freezable system, so the fund should pay for wallets, tooling, off-ramps and liquidity.
questions.prompt: A supporter argued that for someone at risk of debanking, rough UX beats funds that can be frozen or seized (#34). Which is the strongest argument actually made in response, for paying for infrastructure rather than recipients?

questions.explanation: #34 first concedes that UX is rough, then argues that at-risk users still prefer that to frozen funds or a client seeing their USDT balance, and #36 accepts this as the real case for shielded ZEC while arguing it does not justify paying recipients directly. The other options are points made elsewhere: transparency in #47, airdrops in #17, and the no-guarantee point in #7 and #13, the last of which #9 also accepted.
options: That the ZECsy team reports its milestones more transparently than most grantees do.
That for someone at risk of being debanked, rough UX is better than funds that can be frozen or seized.
That airdrops are largely useless because they get farmed and bring little lasting benefit.
That applicants to the fund are not guaranteed any grant and can be rejected.
questions.prompt: In #36 a critic of direct payments granted a point as valid. Which point from #34 was it?
